title: Module 5 · Collaboration, Social Media, and Competitive Position
description: Interactive, case-led module on enhancing collaboration using social media: why organizational communication and collaboration is strategic, virtual teams and synchronous and asynchronous work, collaboration software and videoconferencing, intranets, employee portals and enterprise search, the shift from Web 1.0 to Web 2.0 and user-generated content, blogs, microblogging and instant messaging, media sharing, tagging, geotagging, social bookmarking and cataloging, cloud-based collaboration tools, content and learning management systems, collective intelligence, wikis, open source and crowdsourcing, social networking and viral marketing, the organizational conditions that decide whether an internal social tool succeeds, and the downsides from fake reviews to viral complaints, with supplements reading the whole chapter through the five competitive forces and the value chain and rehearsing the written strategy analysis.

hero:
Module 5

Collaboration, Social Media, and Competitive Position

Module 2 gave you two frameworks and almost nothing to point them at. This module is the material they were built for. Every tool in this chapter — the team meeting held in four time zones, the intranet nobody reads, the review that cost a company a week, the crowd that did the work for two cents a task — changes who holds power over a firm and where inside that firm value is actually created. So you will read the chapter once, and then read it a second time through the five forces and the value chain.

This module is built around one deliverable

The written analysis this course asks for has a fixed shape, and it is the same shape every time: apply the five competitive forces to a firm, use the value chain to find at least two places where information technology could create an advantage, recommend exactly one initiative, and write a short comparison against a company you choose. Everything below is arranged to get you there.

  1. Every section carries a mini case. A short situation, a strip of facts, usually a small exhibit of figures, and two or three decisions to make. The debrief stays shut until you have answered all of them, so the point of the case is worked out rather than read.
  2. Read the short piece first, then work. The prose in each section is deliberately brief. It exists to arm the activity that follows it, not to substitute for it.
  3. Every option explains itself. Including the ones you did not choose. Knowing why a plausible answer is wrong is the part that survives into the next case.
  4. The last two sections are the frameworks. Section 5–4 maps this chapter onto the five forces and the value chain, one tool at a time. Section 5–5 rehearses the whole written deliverable on a hypothetical firm.
  5. Finish with the final challenge. Situations rather than definitions, scored by objective, so a weak area shows up instead of being averaged away.

Where this module sits in the course objectives

The modules follow the textbook’s learning objectives, but the course is graded against a different list of eleven. This table says plainly which of them this module serves and which it leaves to other work, so you always know why you are reading something.

Course objectiveWhat this module does with it
5. Delineate how businesses use internet technology for electronic commerce, communicating with employees and working with business partners This module’s main job. Communicating with employees is the intranet, the employee portal, enterprise search and the internal social network. Working with business partners is the virtual team, the shared document, the videoconference and the extranet-style collaboration that replaced posting drawings back and forth.
3. Discuss how companies use information technology for competitive advantage by changing their marketplace Also central, and the whole of section 5–4. Network effects raise entry barriers, a platform turns its own users into its product, reviews hand power to buyers, and crowdsourcing replaces a category of paid work. Each of those changes a market rather than improving a firm inside one.
2. Discuss how companies use information systems to help manage internal operations and to make decisions Also central. Objective 5.1 is coordination: virtual teams, synchronous against asynchronous work, real-time access to one authoritative document, and employee self-service replacing a paper form that cost tens of dollars to process.
8. Describe the individual and organizational consequences of the use of information technology Substantial, and unusually blunt here. A generation gap inside one workforce, a shift in what people treat as private, anonymity producing behaviour nobody would sign their name to, an algorithm deciding what a person sees, and a complaint reaching millions before the company has read it.
9. Recognize security breaches and computer crimes Substantial. Every tool that widens sharing widens exposure: intellectual property leaving in a shared folder, location metadata a photographer forgot to strip, fake reviews, harassment and doxing, and extremist recruitment running on the same platforms marketing does.
7. Recognize a business problem which might be solved using information technology and then work with the information systems team on a solution Practised end to end in section 5–5, which is a full pass from counted evidence to one recommended initiative with a cost and a measure attached.

The intranet, the firewall it sits behind, the private network that reaches it from a hotel room, and the integration problem every internal tool creates are all this chapter’s, but Modules 1 and 3 are where they are taught.

Coordinate

A team that is never in one room

The right people for a problem are rarely in the same building. Assembling them anyway, and then getting a decision out of them, is what the first half of this chapter is about.

Know

What the company already knows

Large organizations lose their own knowledge constantly. Intranets, search, wikis and internal social networks are all attempts to stop that, and most of them fail for the same reasons.

Reach

A public that answers back

The web stopped being a broadcast. Customers now create the content about you, and the same machinery that carries a marketing campaign carries a complaint.

Position

Forces and value

Every one of those changes moves a competitive force or an activity in the value chain. Naming which one is the difference between an observation and an analysis.

One question runs through the whole module For each tool you meet, ask two things and only two: which force does it move — rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power — and where in the value chain does the work actually happen? A wiki is not a strategy. A wiki that cuts the time an engineer spends re-deriving something a colleague already knew is technology development, and it shows up as a cost the firm’s rivals still pay.

Chapter vocabulary

Every term the chapter defines, written so it makes sense on its own, with an example beside it. Search by word, or filter by the objective the term belongs to. Watch the pairs that sound alike and are not: cooperation and collaboration, a tag and a geotag, a wiki and a content management system, collective intelligence and crowdsourcing, a network effect and critical mass.
finalIntro:
Put it together

Final challenge

Situations rather than definitions. Each one puts you in front of a decision somebody actually has to make — adopt it or refuse it, answer the post or stay quiet, name the force or keep describing the symptom — and asks what is really going on. Every organization described is hypothetical. Answer all of them, then score: the result breaks out by objective, so a weak area points at a section to reread instead of disappearing into one number.
foot: What to do next. Spend a week watching one organization you already belong to — an employer, a team, a club, this course — and write down where its coordination actually breaks. Not the tool it uses; the moment somebody could not find what somebody else already knew, or waited a day for an answer that took ten seconds to give. Then name the force that moment is evidence of, put it somewhere in the value chain, and say what one initiative would change and how you would tell whether it worked. That is the whole method, and it is far easier to practise on an organization you can actually see.
